feature.title: The invention factory
feature.lead: In 1876 Edison built a laboratory whose only job was to invent. A small team of machinists, chemists and a mathematician turned out the telephone transmitter, the phonograph and a whole electric lighting system there, and the idea grew into the much larger West Orange lab.

items.label: The Menlo Park laboratory
items.text: A two-storey white wooden building, finished on 25 March 1876 for about $2,500, in a hamlet on the railway line. It had its own library and machine shop. Edison promised a minor invention every six weeks and a major one every six months.

items.label: The team
items.text: Machinist John Kruesi built the models, Charles Batchelor tested and improved them, and mathematician Francis Upton did the calculations. Francis Jehl, John Ott and others joined them. By spring 1878 the staff had grown to about 25, often working 80-hour weeks.

items.label: Carbon telephone transmitter
items.text: A button of carbon under the diaphragm changed the electric current as the voice pressed on it, making telephone speech much louder. Carbon buttons were made at the lab from lampblack scraped from kerosene lamp chimneys. The basic design stayed in use until the 1980s.

items.label: Tinfoil phonograph
items.text: Edison sketched a grooved cylinder wrapped in tinfoil. John Kruesi built it, thinking the idea absurd. Edison recited 'Mary had a little lamb' and the machine played it back. It was the first machine that could both record and play back sound.

items.label: Electric pen and stencil
items.text: A pen with a tiny motor that punched rows of holes in paper as you wrote, making a stencil for printing many copies. Later work on stencils (US 224,665) fed into office copying machines.

items.label: Practical light bulb
items.text: Others, such as Joseph Swan, had made glowing lamps before. The Menlo Park team made one practical: a high-resistance carbon filament in a very good vacuum. A test in October 1879 lasted about 13.5 hours. Later, carbonised bamboo lasted more than 1,200 hours.

items.label: Dynamo
items.text: A lamp is useless without power. The lab designed its own generators, and later very large 'jumbo' dynamos for the first permanent power station.

items.label: Meter, fuse and wiring
items.text: Edison copied the gas industry: a central station, underground wires, meters and fixtures. The team designed an electric meter and a fuse to stop overloads and fires, so the light could be sold safely to customers.

items.label: Electric railway
items.text: The team built and ran an experimental electric railway at Menlo Park. The Menlo Park Museum says it became a success in 1881.

items.label: Pearl Street Station
items.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
items.text: The first permanent central power station in the system started on 4 September 1882, lighting 400 lamps for 82 customers in lower Manhattan. By 1884 it served 508 customers and over 10,000 lamps.

items.label: Three-wire system
items.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
items.text: Adding a third, neutral wire let the same copper carry power farther, cutting the cost of the system.

items.label: The Edison effect
items.text: While studying his lamps, Edison noticed current flowing across the vacuum inside a bulb. His patent for a meter using it (US 307,031) is often called the first US patent for an electronic device.

items.label: The West Orange laboratory
items.text: A bigger invention factory: a complex opened in late 1887, about ten times the size of Menlo Park, with buildings for chemistry, metallurgy, photography and more. Factories around it made the products. He worked there until his death.

items.label: Kinetoscope and the Black Maria
items.text: A camera and a peephole viewer for moving pictures. Historians credit W. K. L. Dickson with most of the experimental work. Films were shot in the Black Maria, a tar-paper studio that turned on a track to follow the sun.

items.label: Nickel-iron battery
items.text: A lighter, longer-lasting battery meant for electric cars. It took about ten years and thousands of tests to make it reliable. By then petrol cars had won, but the battery sold widely for industrial uses.

timeline.title: Born in Milan, Ohio
timeline.text: Thomas Alva Edison was born in Milan, Ohio. As a boy he was called Al.

timeline.title: Taught at home
timeline.text: The family moved to Port Huron, Michigan. Edison went to school for only a few months. His mother, a former teacher, taught him at home, and he read widely, including history and science books.

timeline.title: A lab in the cellar
timeline.text: At about ten or eleven he got a copy of Parker's School Philosophy, an elementary physics book, and tried nearly every experiment in it. He kept about 200 bottles of chemicals in the cellar, all labelled 'Poison' so no one would touch them.

timeline.title: Newsboy on the railway
timeline.text: He began selling newspapers and snacks on trains between Port Huron and Detroit. In Detroit he spent hours in the public library. Around this age his hearing began to fail. Edison later blamed a blow or pull by a train worker; his biographer Paul Israel points instead to scarlet fever and ear infections.

timeline.title: A rescue and a trade
timeline.text: He printed a small newspaper, the Grand Trunk Herald, on the train. In August 1862 he pulled the station agent's small son off the track in front of a rolling freight car. The grateful father, J. U. MacKenzie, taught him telegraphy.

timeline.title: Wandering telegrapher
timeline.text: He worked as a night telegrapher at Stratford Junction, Ontario, but left after a near collision blamed on his mistake. Until 1869 he held night telegraph jobs in Ontario, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and Massachusetts. Other operators saw him as bright, but his tinkering sometimes got in the way of his work.

timeline.title: Boston
timeline.text: In Boston he made some money from a stock ticker for local customers, then lost it trying to expand to New York. He began inventing in earnest at a local telegraph workshop.

timeline.title: First patent, first lesson
timeline.text: He received his first patent, US 90,646, for an electric vote recorder. Congress did not want it, because slow voting helped the minority. He decided to invent only things people truly needed.

timeline.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
timeline.title: Inventor for hire
timeline.text: He moved to New York nearly penniless, then went into business with Franklin Leonard Pope as electrical engineers. He improved stock and gold printing telegraphs, and soon opened shops in Newark, New Jersey.

timeline.title: Marries Mary Stilwell
timeline.text: He married Mary Stilwell, 16, who worked in one of his shops. They had three children. Charles Batchelor, an English machinist, was by then working with him and became his chief experimental assistant in 1873.

timeline.title: The quadruplex
timeline.text: He sold his quadruplex telegraph, which sent four messages over one wire at once, for $30,000. The money helped pay for a new laboratory.

timeline.title: The invention factory opens
timeline.text: His laboratory at Menlo Park was finished. It was a place built only to invent, with a library, a machine shop and a team. It became a model for later industrial research labs.

timeline.title: A louder telephone
timeline.text: For Western Union he developed a carbon telephone transmitter, testing many materials. It made phone speech much clearer and louder.

timeline.title: The phonograph
timeline.text: Edison announced a machine that recorded and played back sound, and showed it on 29 November. Sources differ on the exact days it was built and first shown. In April 1878 he demonstrated it to the National Academy of Sciences, and the press named him 'The Wizard of Menlo Park'.

timeline.title: A lamp that lasts
timeline.text: A carbon filament lamp burned for about 13.5 hours. Sources give 21 or 22 October. He filed his lamp patent on 4 November; US 223,898 was granted on 27 January 1880.

timeline.title: Menlo Park lit up
timeline.text: Crowds came by train to see the laboratory and nearby street lit by electric lamps in public demonstrations at the end of the year.

timeline.title: Iron from sand
timeline.text: He patented a magnetic ore separator and began trying to pull iron from beach sand. It was the start of a long mining project.

timeline.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
timeline.title: Pearl Street
timeline.text: His Pearl Street Station began supplying direct current to customers in lower Manhattan. It was the first permanent central station of his system, after an earlier station at Holborn Viaduct in London that January.

timeline.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
timeline.title: New faces
timeline.text: Nikola Tesla worked at the Edison Machine Works for about six months, improving dynamos; he may have met Edison only a few times. Lewis Latimer, an expert in carbon filaments, joined the Edison company as a draftsman and patent expert.

timeline.title: Mary dies
timeline.text: His wife Mary died at 29. Their daughter Marion remembered her father shaking with grief.

timeline.title: Marries Mina Miller
timeline.text: He married Mina Miller and bought Glenmont, a house in West Orange, New Jersey. They had three children. He had also bought land in Fort Myers, Florida, for a winter home.

timeline.title: A bigger lab
timeline.text: His new West Orange laboratory opened, about ten times the size of Menlo Park. He called on it to tackle the research needs of modern industry.

timeline.title: War of the currents
timeline.text: Edison backed direct current and warned that Westinghouse's alternating current was deadly. Harold Brown, who received help from Edison's lab, killed animals with AC in public tests. Westinghouse licensed Tesla's AC motor patents that July. AC won out in the end, and the contest was mainly between companies, not two men.

timeline.title: Moving pictures
timeline.text: A prototype Kinetoscope was shown to about 150 visitors. W. K. L. Dickson did most of the experimental work. The finished viewer premiered in Brooklyn in May 1893, with films shot in the Black Maria studio.

timeline.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
timeline.title: General Electric
timeline.text: Financiers merged Edison General Electric with Thomson-Houston to form General Electric, run by Thomson-Houston managers. Edison, who had already lost control, learned of it only a day before. His name was dropped.

timeline.title: The ore mill fails
timeline.text: After about eleven years and more than $2 million of his own money, he gave up his iron ore mill. New ore fields near the Great Lakes made his ore too expensive. He reused the crushing machines to make cement.

timeline.title: The storage battery
timeline.text: He patented a nickel-iron battery and founded the Edison Storage Battery Company. It took about ten years of testing to make it reliable.

timeline.title: The fire
timeline.text: A fire destroyed thirteen buildings of his works and killed one employee. He rebuilt and kept working.

timeline.title: Naval Consulting Board
timeline.text: During the First World War he headed the Naval Consulting Board, a group of scientists and industrialists advising the US Navy.

timeline.title: Rubber from plants
timeline.text: His last big project searched for a home-grown source of rubber. He and his team tested about 17,000 plant samples and settled on a goldenrod.

timeline.title: Congressional Gold Medal
timeline.text: He received the Congressional Gold Medal. President Coolidge joined the ceremony by radio.

timeline.title: Light's Golden Jubilee
timeline.text: On the 50th anniversary of his lamp, Edison and his former assistant Francis Jehl re-enacted the lamp test in Henry Ford's rebuilt Menlo Park laboratory, with President Hoover present.

timeline.title: Death at Glenmont
timeline.text: Edison died at his home, Glenmont, at 84. He held 1,093 US patents.

timeline.title: A minute of darkness
timeline.text: At President Hoover's request, many people across the country turned off their lights for one minute in his honour.

timeline.title: A national park
timeline.text: His West Orange laboratory and Glenmont, protected since 1956, became Thomas Edison National Historical Park.

patentsNote: Edison held 1,093 US patents (Wikipedia); this list shows a selection of 39 significant ones, from his first (the vote recorder) to one granted after his death (US 1,908,830, 1933). Titles and grant dates come from each Google Patents record. Google Patents gives no filing date in its data for many 19th-century patents, so the filing date was read from the 'Application filed' line in the patent text it shows; a null filing date means none could be read (US 90,646, 96,567, 158,787 and 203,013 show none, and the scan of US 228,329 reads '1830', a scanning error, so it is left blank). Some patents were granted many years after filing, such as the carbon transmitter (US 474,230, filed 1877, granted 1892) and the duplex telegraph (US 480,567, filed 1874, granted 1892). Many of these patents were assigned to his companies or backers, such as Western Union and the Edison Electric Light Company, and much of the work behind them was done by his staff.

works.title: Electric vote recorder
works.text: His first patent (US 90,646): lawmakers press a switch and the votes are counted at once. Congress did not want it.

works.title: Stock and gold printers
works.text: Improved printing telegraphs that printed prices on paper tape for brokers and traders (for example US 96,567).

works.title: Quadruplex telegraph
works.text: Sent four messages over one wire at once, two each way, saving telegraph companies the cost of new wires.

works.title: Electric pen
works.text: A motor-driven pen that punched a stencil as you wrote, for printing many copies of a letter (US 180,857).

works.title: Carbon telephone transmitter
works.text: A carbon button that made telephone voices louder and clearer; the basic design lasted about a century.

works.title: Tinfoil phonograph
works.text: The first machine to record and play back sound, built by machinist John Kruesi from Edison's sketch (US 200,521).

works.title: Practical incandescent lamp
works.text: A high-resistance carbon filament in a high vacuum, built to work inside a full power system (US 223,898).

works.title: Dynamo
works.text: Efficient generators designed for the lighting system, later scaled up into 'jumbo' dynamos for Pearl Street (US 219,393).

works.title: Electric light and power system
works.text: Central station, underground wires, meters, fuses and lamps, first running permanently at Pearl Street in New York.

works.title: Three-wire distribution
works.text: A third, neutral wire that let the system reach farther with less copper (US 274,290).

works.title: The Edison effect
works.text: Current flowing through the vacuum in a lamp, used in a meter patent often called the first US patent for an electronic device (US 307,031).

works.title: Improved phonograph
works.text: One of his improved phonograph designs from the new West Orange laboratory (US 386,974).

works.title: Kinetograph and Kinetoscope
works.text: A motion-picture camera and peephole viewer, developed largely by W. K. L. Dickson in Edison's lab (US 493,426).

works.title: Introduction to the Kineto-Phonograph
works.text: Edison's short signed introduction in Century Magazine, crediting the zoetrope toy, Muybridge, Marey (he spells it Marié) and Dickson.

works.title: Magnetic ore milling
works.text: A giant plant to separate iron ore with magnets. It cost him over $2 million and failed, but its rock crushers moved into cement.

works.title: Nickel-iron storage battery
works.text: A rugged alkaline battery, reliable after about ten years of testing, sold for many industrial uses (US 678,722).

works.title: Portland cement kilns
works.text: Kiln equipment for his Edison Portland Cement Company, founded in 1899 (US 802,631).

works.title: Rubber from goldenrod
works.text: A search through about 17,000 plants for rubber that could be grown in the United States (US 1,740,079).
